newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria's Vranitzky says failed to block far right.
newsitem.headline: Austria's Vranitzky says failed to block far right.

text.p: Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky, who has announced he is resigning, said on Sunday his greatest achievement in nearly 11 years in power was to lead Austria into the European Union.
But he conceded at a news conference that his Social Democratic Party had underestimated the politicial rise of the far right under the leadership of nationalist Joerg Haider.
While Vranitzky relaxed answering reporters' questions and cracking jokes, no one could pinpoint the whereabouts of his designated successor, Finance Minister Viktor Klima.

Vranitzky made the surprise announcement of his resignation on Saturday after an emergency meeting of the Social Democratic Party leadership and passed the chancellor's baton to an apparently reluctant Klima.

"I think my greatest success was to take Austria into the European Union," he told the news conference, adding that one of his greatest challenges was to cope with the changing face of Europe in the post-Cold War period.

More than two-thirds of the Austrian electorate voted in favour of EU membership in June 1994, but disillusionment has set in following big cuts in public spending to prepare Austria for European economic and monetary union.
Vranitzky, 59, said he also took pride in turning around the economy of the Alpine nation from its depressed state in the 1970s to one of Europe's best performers.

Rounding off his valedictory statement to the press, the soft-spoken chancellor acknowledged that he had gone some way to tackling the difficult relationship many Austrians had with their wartime past as part of Hitler's Third Reich.

Vranitzky made a memorable speech to parliament in 1991 in which he soberly told deputies that their country had to apologise to Jews for Austria's part in the horrors committed by the World War Two Nazi regime.
In a visit to Israel in 1993, Vranitzky said Austrians, too, had to share responsibility for the Nazi Holocaust.

The choice of 49-year-old Klima received the thumbs-up from much of the Austrian press. "Klima represents continuity but with different means. He is cleverer, more capable of getting the desired results and has a better instinct for power," the daily Kurier said in an editorial.

Vranitzky, who took over the government in June 1986, said his leadership also had its downs and his party had failed to mount an appropriate strategy to combat the growing popularity of Haider's far-right Freedom Party.
And with hindsight, he said he would have handled Haider differently.
"Perhaps the Social Democrats were a bit too late and did not do enough to unmask his strategy of demonising human beings or organisations," Vranitzky said.
Vranitzky and Haider took over their respective parties within months of each other in 1986.

While the Social Democrat vote slumped to an all-time low in European elections last October, dipping below 30 percent, support for the far right has soared to nearly 28 percent from the nine percent it garnered before Haider took over.
Vranitzky said he finally made his mind up to call it a day in the first half of last week, but stressed that his only reason to quit was to hand over his office to a younger person.

His decision followed a bitter row with the conservatives led by Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schuessel over the sale of the country's second biggest bank -- one of many rows which have shaken the coalition over the past two years.
